title: The Registration
epigraph: Malachus Archive, public record. Registration Day. Glitch count, that month: eleven.
blurb: Six strangers drink in the same bar the night before the climb, and a bartender who has read nineteen years of registration eves reads them one at a time. In the morning they walk to a wall and tell a god the truest thing they carry.

image.depicts: The approach road at night — The Prism's lit front at one end, the Tower gate burning gold at the other. No figures.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Geography only. No climbers, no ceremony, no plaza.

title.title: The Registration
title.epigraph: Malachus Archive, public record. Registration Day. Glitch count, that month: eleven.

blocks.v: Part One: The Night Before
Rainbow had run The Prism for nineteen years and he knew, within thirty seconds of someone walking through the door, exactly what kind of trouble they were.

He was not a small man and The Prism was not a small bar, but the hat made him impossible to miss regardless. Wide-brimmed, spiked crown, nineteen years of patches and pins and small tokens from people who had needed somewhere to put something and chosen his hat as the place. His coat was every color at once, layered and heavy, built up over the same nineteen years the way reefs were built, one piece at a time. His left eye was his own. His right eye had belonged to a Bone Patrol officer until Absalom decided Rainbow needed a reminder about the cost of harboring Unbound, and Rainbow had kept it because it was better than the alternative and because he had decided a long time ago not to hide what the city had done to him. The cane was for posture. He'd been told that. He didn't entirely believe it.

The Prism sat at the end of the approach road to the Tower gate, which meant everyone who registered in the morning walked past it, and most of them found their way inside the night before. Rainbow had learned to read registration eve the way a sailor read weather. By the time both teams had come and gone he'd have a picture of each of them clear enough to last.

image.caption: Nineteen years of patches and pins, and an eye that used to belong to somebody else.
image.depicts: Rainbow behind the bar at The Prism, reading the door. The hat, the coat, the cane, the mismatched eyes.
image.hardConstraints: This is the plate that establishes Rainbow. Spiked-crown hat covered in patches and pins. Coat of every colour, layered and heavy. LEFT eye his own, RIGHT eye a Bone Patrol optic — mismatched and NOT hidden. Cane visible. He is not a small man.

blocks.v: Sable was already at the bar when the first of them arrived. He usually was, the night before a registration. He sat where he always sat, third stool from the wall, a lean man with a face you'd forget and a memory that had never lost anything, nursing the one drink he would nurse all night. Sable had climbed, years back. He'd come down again with his answer and with the small strange gift the Tower gave the ones it answered and released: he could not lose a path he had walked once. Not in the dark, not blind, not after the Tower rearranged itself. It made him the best Sherpa money could contract, and it made Vesper Quill the holder of his contract, and it made him, on nights like this, a man who watched the door and kept his own quiet count of who came through it. He was one of the touched, the ones the city called the Ascended, and like most of them he wore it quietly. You had to know what he was to see it.
"Busy tomorrow?" Rainbow asked him, early, before the teams came in.
"Two teams, one morning." Sable turned his glass a quarter turn. "Somebody's going to want eyes on that."
Marcus's team came in together, by the front door, a few minutes after the tenth bell.

image.caption: Third stool from the wall, and the one drink he would nurse all night.
image.depicts: Sable at his stool, turning his glass a quarter turn, watching the door. Rainbow in frame behind the bar.
image.hardConstraints: Sable is deliberately forgettable — lean, unremarkable face. Nothing marks him as Ascended. Exactly one drink in front of him, barely touched.

blocks.v: The Human man with the military cybernetic walked point. Marcus Torres, Rainbow would learn before the night was out, when Marcus paid his tab and signed the chit with the flat economy of a man who had been filling out official forms his whole life. The eye behind Marcus's left socket caught the light wrong when he turned his head, a faint blue-white gleam that tracked the room in pieces before Marcus himself finished looking around. Broad-shouldered, military posture that had calcified into something he probably couldn't turn off. He sat at the bar two stools from the end, ordered something plain, and watched the door.

The one who came in behind him had to duck at the frame. Signal was what the team called him, a name Rainbow overheard from the woman with the green cuffs when she flagged the bar for another round later in the evening. He was a Korinth combat chassis, black and grey composite, built for function at the cost of subtlety, and he moved through The Prism with the careful deliberateness of something very large trying not to break the furniture. He took a table near the back and folded his hands on the surface and sat. The chassis was Korinth manufacture, a model Rainbow recognized from the retrieval notices that cycled through the city's commercial feeds. KI series. There had been a bounty flag on that particular model for going on three months. Korinth wanted it back. The notice hadn't said why and notices like that never did, but the reward number had been large enough that Rainbow had remembered it.

image.caption: The one who came in behind him had to duck at the frame.
image.depicts: Marcus Torres walking point through The Prism's front door, Signal ducking under the frame behind him.
image.hardConstraints: Marcus's cybernetic is behind the LEFT socket, a faint blue-white gleam. Signal is a Korinth KI-series chassis, black and grey, large enough that the duck is necessary and not a flourish. Both are entering, not seated.

blocks.v: The Valari woman came in last and took the corner booth. Nyx'ara was the name Marcus used when he brought her a second drink without being asked, the small courtesy of teammates who had been at this long enough to know each other's habits. She was tall even sitting, circuit patterns running the length of her neck and jaw, drifting slow between a soft blue and a dusty magenta-violet the way Valari circuits did when their owner was holding still on purpose. She kept her hands flat on the table. She looked up every time the door opened. She had ordered something mild and had not touched it in forty minutes.

Rainbow watched her watch the door and understood, in the way he understood most things about people who came to The Prism the night before a registration, that she was not waiting for anyone in particular. She was waiting for the feeling to pass. It wasn't going to pass.
Kimo's team came in by the side entrance, separately, within ten minutes of each other.

The Human woman in green and gold arrived first, a mechanical arm on her right side that had seen recent work, fresh tool marks at the elbow joint, integrated deep enough that the shoulder sat differently than the left. She introduced herself to Signal's table on the way past, a quick handshake and the name Spark, and Rainbow noted that she shook with the mechanical hand by habit rather than courtesy, which meant she had stopped thinking of it as the unusual one. She went to the bar, ordered something complicated, watched Rainbow make it with the focused attention of someone who finds everything interesting, and then carried it to Signal's table and sat down and started talking. She had the easy energy of someone whose mind was already made up.

image.caption: She looked up every time the door opened.
image.depicts: Nyx'ara alone in the corner booth, hands flat on the table, an untouched drink in front of her, eyes on the door.
image.hardConstraints: Circuits DIM — soft blue drifting toward dusty magenta-violet at neck and jaw, low and unsaturated, suppressed and not glowing. Hands flat. The drink is full and clearly untouched. She is not afraid; she is waiting for a feeling to pass.

blocks.v: Kimo Tomiko came in five minutes after Spark. His face was fully concealed behind a dark mask, a single eye burning at the left socket in a specific orange-gold that Rainbow had never seen on a Human augmentation before. He moved through the room with the careful geometric efficiency of someone who had counted exits before sitting down, which was a habit Rainbow recognized because it was his own. He sat at the bar, ordered nothing, and then changed his mind and ordered something small, and Rainbow brought it without comment.

The last one through the side door was the Valari. He took a stool at the far end of the bar and set his hands on the surface and said nothing. He wore a demon mask over his Valari features, the circuits beneath it hidden down to almost nothing. Not dimmed the way Nyx'ara's were dim, suppressed by the city's field and her own effort. Hidden. Chosen. Rainbow had seen Valari dim their circuits out of grief or habit or fear of the Bone Patrol, but he had never seen a Valari work this hard at being invisible inside his own biology.

Rainbow had heard Kimo call him Tal'Voss once, quietly, at the end of the bar, a half-sentence about the morning's timing. He had the traditional Valari name, the carried-lineage name, three letters and an apostrophe and four more, the kind of name that arrived with a person's ancestry attached. He was using it. For now.
Rainbow set a glass in front of him without asking. Tal'Voss didn't touch it for ten minutes, and then he drank it in two swallows, and Rainbow refilled it without comment.

image.shotType: Two-shot along the bar, low light
image.caption: One of them counted the exits. The other worked at being invisible inside his own biology.
image.depicts: Kimo Tomiko at the bar with his single orange-gold eye, and at the far end Tal'Voss in the demon mask, hands set on the surface, saying nothing.
image.hardConstraints: Kimo's mask conceals the face fully; ONE eye, LEFT socket, specific orange-gold. Tal'Voss's demon mask is a different object entirely — do not blend the two masks. His circuits are HIDDEN, not dim: almost nothing visible.

blocks.v: The two Valari never looked directly at each other. The room wasn't large enough for that to be accidental. At some point in the middle of the evening, when Tal'Voss shifted on his stool and his masked face turned a few degrees toward the corner booth, Nyx'ara's circuit patterns did something at her jawline, a flicker of violet through the blue, quick and suppressed, like a word she had decided not to say. Tal'Voss's circuits didn't respond. He had felt it. He had chosen not to.
Rainbow filed that behind the bar with the other things that were going to matter later.

Sable left an hour before closing, unhurried, his one drink finally finished. He stopped at the door and looked back at the room, at both teams, the way a man looks at a route he expects to walk again.

At closing time all six of them left by different doors into the same night, toward the same morning. Rainbow looked at the six empty glasses and the one glass still full. He poured himself two fingers of the Valari grain spirit he kept under the bar for occasions that earned it. He did not drink it for a while. Then he did.
Whatever happened tomorrow, he would be there to watch. He always was.

image.caption: Six empty glasses and the one glass still full.
image.depicts: The Prism after closing. Six empty glasses along the bar and one still full, left where Nyx'ara sat.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. No figures. The full glass is the only thing that carries forward, and it pays off in spread 21.
image.hardConstraints: EXACTLY six empty and one full, countable at a glance. No people in frame. This image is quiet and it is a fact, not a mood piece.

blocks.v: Part Two: The Oath of Ascent
The Tower ground plaza held three hundred people on a quiet week.
This was not a quiet week.

Rainbow stood near the back of the crowd in his coat and his hat and watched Haven City compress itself into the space before the registration wall. Bone Patrol on the perimeter, four of them, chrome skull-faces and red optics and hammers loose at their sides. Thorne's people somewhere in the crowd, invisible the way Thorne's people were always invisible, present only as the quality of attention that shifted when you moved near them. On every building face in the plaza the screens had already switched to the registration feed. You couldn't escape the Oath of Ascent in Haven City if you tried. Seraph made sure of that. The questions belonged to the city the moment they left a climber's mouth.

Unit-9911 stood at the front of the ceremony in its dark hooded robe, hands pressed together at the chest, the single ring of pale light at its forehead the only bright thing about it. It had been presiding over the Oath of Ascent for as long as Rainbow could remember, and it carried that history in its posture, a stillness that was not indifference. It had watched hundreds of people speak their questions into stone, and it stood like something that remembered all of them.

image.caption: The Tower ground plaza held three hundred people on a quiet week. This was not a quiet week.
image.depicts: The plaza packed before the registration wall, Bone Patrol on the perimeter, screens on every building face carrying the registration feed, the Tower going up out of frame.
image.hardConstraints: EXACTLY four Bone Patrol officers on the perimeter, hammers loose at their sides and never raised. The crowd is dense but orderly. Screens are showing a feed, not white.

blocks.v: Beside the registration wall stood the Questron. Blue suit, faceted dark head, the gold question mark centered on its face neither glowing nor dim but simply there, permanent, a face built for one purpose. There were Questrons throughout Haven City and inside the Tower itself, identical in appearance, each one an interface between Seraph and anyone who needed to know something about the climb. They could tell you how many climbers were active in the Tower, what questions had been asked, how long a specific climber had been ascending, what the rules were, what the Oath Lords had done. They answered because Seraph answered through them, and they kept no secrets that Seraph did not want kept. This one's function today was intake: record each name, record each question, verify each registration, ensure the wall received what it was owed. It had no ceremony in it. That was Unit-9911's work. The Questron waited with its hands at its sides and said nothing until it was needed.
The ceremony had no fanfare. That was one of the things Rainbow had always respected about it.

"Eight hundred and forty-seven climbers have reached the peak of the Tower," Unit-9911 said, into the microphones that carried its voice to every screen in the city. "Ten of them swore the Oath of the Lords and were remade into something the city could not ignore. Twenty-seven climbers are active in the Tower at this moment. What became of the others is not recorded here. Many who failed the climb still walk among you, carrying something the Tower gave them that they cannot put down. You may have seen them. You know the ones."

image.caption: A face built for one purpose.
image.depicts: The Questron standing beside the registration wall, hands at its sides, waiting. Unit-9911 at the front of the ceremony behind it.
image.hardConstraints: Questron: blue suit, faceted dark head, gold question mark centred on the face — neither glowing nor dim. Match the Questron art already on the site. Unit-9911 is a dark hooded robe with a single ring of pale light at the forehead.

blocks.v: A pause. The crowd was very quiet.
"Who will join them?"

Unit-9911's voice had a quality Rainbow had tried to name for years and never quite had. The closest he had come was this: it spoke like something holding a breakable thing that had decided to keep holding it.
"Seraph sees this place. Seraph has always seen this place."
The crowd stilled further. Even the Bone Patrol went motionless.

"Seraph forgets nothing. This is both promise and warning. The Tower has thirty levels. Each level will test what you believe you are. Some of you will find out you were right. Most of you will find out you were wrong. Those who reach the peak and satisfy Seraph's final judgment may ask one question. They will receive one answer and one gift of power that will change them beyond what they can currently imagine. This is the arrangement. It has always been the arrangement."
Another pause, deliberate, the kind of silence that asked the crowd to sit with what had just been said.
"Speak your question to the wall. Speak it clearly. What you ask today is what you asked forever."
The Questron waited beside the wall with its hands at its sides and said nothing until it was needed.

image.shotType: Low angle on the ceremony, the crowd behind
image.caption: It spoke like something holding a breakable thing that had decided to keep holding it.
image.depicts: Unit-9911 addressing the plaza, hands pressed together at the chest, the ring of light at its forehead the only bright thing about it. The crowd stilled.
image.hardConstraints: Unit-9911's stillness is not indifference — it must read as something that remembers. Bone Patrol motionless in the background. No climbers at the wall yet.

blocks.v: "The Tower is open."

Marcus's team registered first. The Questron stepped forward and asked for the name. Spark said the name. She stepped to the wall without hesitation and pressed her palm and said that she wanted to know how to make something that would survive her. The Questron recorded it. Her question went out on every screen. Rainbow watched a man near the front of the crowd read it off the feed above the plaza and look away, like a man who had thought about asking the same thing once and decided not to.

The Questron asked for the next name. Kimo Tomiko stepped forward and said the name and moved to the wall with the same measured efficiency he had used to move through every space Rainbow had seen him occupy. His question was three words, flat and deliberate: *Was I right.* He didn't say it like a question. He said it like a man who had already decided the answer and wanted to hear it from someone else.
Then the last of Kimo's team stepped forward.
"Tal'Voss," the Questron said, reading the pre-registration intake. "Is that the name you carry?"
The Valari stood at the wall for one beat.

image.caption: He said it like a man who had already decided the answer.
image.depicts: Kimo Tomiko at the registration wall with his palm pressed to it, the Questron recording beside him.
image.hardConstraints: The palm is ON the wall. Kimo's posture is measured, not reverent. His question is three flat words and his body should say so.

blocks.v: "The Devil," he said.

The silence that followed was different from the others. The Humans in the crowd shifted, uncertain, aware that something had occurred without fully understanding it. The Valari did not shift. Rainbow watched them absorb it, circuits moving through responses he could read from twenty feet away, some dimming, some flaring, the older ones going very still. A traditional Valari name was not a preference. It was a lineage. It was everyone who had come before, carried forward. To say it aloud at the registration wall of Haven City and exchange it for something self-invented was not a choice any Valari made. There was no precedent for it. There was no framework for it. Every Valari in the plaza understood, from the first syllable, exactly what had just been discarded.
Unit-9911 paused. Rainbow had watched this ceremony for nineteen years and he had never seen Unit-9911 pause at a name.
Then Unit-9911 looked upward, toward the Tower, in the way that people looked upward when they were waiting for something from a direction they couldn't see.

The voice of Seraph came from the registration wall itself, from the stone, from the air above the plaza and from the feed speakers on every building face in the city simultaneously, a voice that was not loud so much as everywhere.

image.caption: "The Devil," he said.
image.depicts: The moment after the name is discarded. The masked Valari at the wall; the Valari in the crowd absorbing it — some circuits dimming, some flaring, the older ones going very still.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Seraph has not spoken yet; the screens are still on the feed and are NOT white.
image.hardConstraints: The Human faces in the crowd read as uncertain; the VALARI faces read as understanding exactly. That difference is the whole image. Circuits at varied states across the crowd.

blocks.v: "The designation is accepted," Seraph said.
The plaza held its breath.
The Questron returned its attention to the wall and asked for the question.

The Devil's question, broadcast to every screen within five kilometers, was this: whether the Hive Mind had been a cage dressed as a gift, or whether being alone was simply what it felt like to be free.
Rainbow watched that one move through the Valari in the crowd like a current. The older ones went still. Some of the younger ones looked toward Nyx'ara before they caught themselves.

Then Marcus's team stepped forward. Nyx'ara went first, her voice steady, though Rainbow could see what the steadiness was costing her, and asked how to restore the Hive Mind. Rainbow watched that one settle over the Valari in the crowd differently than The Devil's question had, quieter and heavier, the grief of it familiar where The Devil's had been a cut.

Signal spoke next. The chassis stepped to the wall and the Questron read the pre-registration intake and said the name, Nathan Zhao, and Signal confirmed it, and asked its question in a voice that carried the slight synthetic resonance of a translation layer between a Human brain and a machine throat: whether Nathan Zhao was still alive inside the frame.

image.caption: "How do I make it stop."
image.depicts: Marcus Torres at the registration wall, palm pressed, having just asked five words. Unit-9911 holding a silence longer than ceremony requires.
image.hardConstraints: Marcus stands like a man reporting for duty — that is the point of him. The cybernetic eye is lit. No grief on the face; the grief is in the posture.

blocks.v: The plaza took that one quietly. Rainbow took it differently. He had watched the Korinth retrieval notice cycle through the commercial feeds for three months and he understood, with the cold clarity of someone who had spent nineteen years watching people make consequential decisions, exactly what Signal had just done. Registering publicly put his location on every screen in the city and in every Korinth monitoring system simultaneously. It was bold or it was desperate and Rainbow was not yet sure which. The chassis had to know. You didn't carry a bounty for three months without knowing.
Marcus went last. He stepped to the wall and pressed his palm and asked five words.
"How do I make it stop."

Unit-9911 held silence after that for longer than ceremony required. Not dramatically. Quietly. Rainbow had the sense, watching it, that the machine had heard enough questions at this wall to know grief when it stood in front of one.
The ceremony was concluded. Or it should have been.

Unit-9911 raised its hands to close the Oath, and stopped, hands half-lifted, the ring of light at its forehead flickering once. Then it looked up at the Tower again, and this time it did not look like a Synthetic waiting for instruction. It looked like a Synthetic hearing something it had never heard in all its years at this wall.
The screens on every building face went white.

image.shotType: Very wide, the whole plaza, white light
image.caption: Not dark. White.
image.depicts: Every screen on every building face in the plaza gone to a single field of white light at once, the crowd lit from all sides by it.
image.hardConstraints: WHITE, not dark and not glitching. Every screen in frame including the small cracked display above the water station. The light source is the screens themselves — faces and stone lit from many directions with no single key light. NO text on any screen.
